cards.explanation: Defining the population makes it possible to interpret frequencies and compare risks.
cards.text: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health events in defined {{c1::populations}}.
cards.question: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health events in defined {{c1::populations}}.

cards.explanation: An isolated count rarely shows whether the observed experience differs from expectation.
cards.text: To judge whether a health outcome is unusually frequent, an investigator needs a valid {{c1::comparison group}}.
cards.question: To judge whether a health outcome is unusually frequent, an investigator needs a valid {{c1::comparison group}}.

cards.explanation: These dimensions help identify groups at risk and generate hypotheses.
cards.text: In descriptive epidemiology, patterns of disease are organised by person, place and {{c1::time}}.
cards.question: In descriptive epidemiology, patterns of disease are organised by person, place and {{c1::time}}.

cards.explanation: A large city may have more cases but a lower risk per resident.
cards.text: Comparing case counts between cities requires a denominator representing the {{c1::population at risk}}.
cards.question: Comparing case counts between cities requires a denominator representing the {{c1::population at risk}}.

cards.explanation: Analytical studies test whether such factors help explain an observed distribution.
cards.text: An exposure that influences the occurrence of disease is an epidemiological {{c1::determinant}}.
cards.question: An exposure that influences the occurrence of disease is an epidemiological {{c1::determinant}}.

cards.explanation: Understanding that course helps interpret prognosis and identify opportunities for prevention.
cards.text: The course a disease takes over time in the absence of intervention is its {{c1::natural history}}.
cards.question: The course a disease takes over time in the absence of intervention is its {{c1::natural history}}.

cards.explanation: This matters when disease risk changes substantially with age.
cards.text: Age-adjusted rates compare populations after accounting for differences in their {{c1::age distributions}}.
cards.question: Age-adjusted rates compare populations after accounting for differences in their {{c1::age distributions}}.

cards.explanation: Deaths from breast cancer contribute instead to the cause-specific mortality rate.
cards.text: New breast cancer diagnoses contribute to the {{c1::incidence}} rate.
cards.question: New breast cancer diagnoses contribute to the {{c1::incidence}} rate.

cards.explanation: Testing and reporting practices affect counts.
cards.text: A map of confirmed cases alone cannot distinguish higher disease risk from more intensive {{c1::case detection}}.
cards.question: A map of confirmed cases alone cannot distinguish higher disease risk from more intensive {{c1::case detection}}.

cards.explanation: Describing who was affected and identifying causes precede the public health action.
cards.text: Using findings from an outbreak investigation to prevent more cases is the {{c1::application}} component of epidemiology.
cards.question: Using findings from an outbreak investigation to prevent more cases is the {{c1::application}} component of epidemiology.

cards.explanation: Mapping cases helped generate a hypothesis about the Broad Street pump.
cards.text: John Snow linked cholera cases in Soho to a shared {{c1::water supply}}.
cards.question: John Snow linked cholera cases in Soho to a shared {{c1::water supply}}.

cards.explanation: A spatial cluster can generate a hypothesis. It does not by itself quantify an exposure effect.
cards.text: Snow’s map of cholera cases around water pumps illustrates {{c1::descriptive epidemiology}}.
cards.question: Snow’s map of cholera cases around water pumps illustrates {{c1::descriptive epidemiology}}.

cards.explanation: The water source defines the comparison groups, and mortality is the outcome.
cards.text: Comparing cholera mortality between households supplied by different companies tests an {{c1::exposure hypothesis}}.
cards.question: Comparing cholera mortality between households supplied by different companies tests an {{c1::exposure hypothesis}}.

cards.explanation: Divide the two rates rather than subtracting their case counts.
cards.text: The reported cholera rates were 4.2 and 0.5 deaths per 1,000. The higher rate was about {{c1::8.4 times}} the lower rate.
cards.question: The reported cholera rates were 4.2 and 0.5 deaths per 1,000. The higher rate was about {{c1::8.4 times}} the lower rate.

cards.explanation: Examples include improving access to preventive services and identifying communities at elevated risk.
cards.text: The unit of concern in public health is the {{c1::population}}.
cards.question: The unit of concern in public health is the {{c1::population}}.

cards.explanation: The other core functions include policy development and assurance.
cards.text: Monitoring community health to identify problems and priorities is the public health function of {{c1::assessment}}.
cards.question: Monitoring community health to identify problems and priorities is the public health function of {{c1::assessment}}.

cards.explanation: It can inform diagnosis, prognosis and treatment.
cards.text: Clinical epidemiology applies population-based evidence to decisions about {{c1::individual patients}}.
cards.question: Clinical epidemiology applies population-based evidence to decisions about {{c1::individual patients}}.

cards.explanation: Clinical epidemiology also uses population evidence, but applies it to patient care.
cards.text: Classical epidemiology investigates risk factors in communities to guide {{c1::prevention}}.
cards.question: Classical epidemiology investigates risk factors in communities to guide {{c1::prevention}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Observation can still test an analytical hypothesis about smoking and health.
cards.text: When investigators record smoking habits without assigning anyone to smoke, the study is {{c1::observational}}.
cards.question: When investigators record smoking habits without assigning anyone to smoke, the study is {{c1::observational}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Differences between the strata may be hidden in an overall estimate.
cards.text: Examining an association separately in different age groups is called {{c1::stratification}}.
cards.question: Examining an association separately in different age groups is called {{c1::stratification}}.

cards.explanation: Controls should represent the population from which the cases arose.
cards.text: A study that selects people by disease status and compares prior exposures uses a {{c1::case–control}} design.
cards.question: A study that selects people by disease status and compares prior exposures uses a {{c1::case–control}} design.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Selecting controls solely for convenience can distort their exposure distribution.
cards.text: Controls in a case–control study should come from the population that produced the {{c1::cases}}.
cards.question: Controls in a case–control study should come from the population that produced the {{c1::cases}}.

cards.explanation: The groups provide denominators for estimating risk.
cards.text: A study that groups participants by exposure and compares subsequent outcomes is a {{c1::cohort study}}.
cards.question: A study that groups participants by exposure and compares subsequent outcomes is a {{c1::cohort study}}.

cards.explanation: Its defining feature is that the comparison starts with exposure groups.
cards.text: A cohort reconstructed from records after the outcomes occurred is {{c1::retrospective}}.
cards.question: A cohort reconstructed from records after the outcomes occurred is {{c1::retrospective}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The outcome is ascertained after follow-up begins.
cards.text: Following known exposure groups forward from enrolment to observe new events is a {{c1::prospective cohort}} design.
cards.question: Following known exposure groups forward from enrolment to observe new events is a {{c1::prospective cohort}} design.

cards.explanation: The sample may distort the association in the source population.
cards.text: Systematic differences in who enters a study can introduce {{c1::selection bias}}.
cards.question: Systematic differences in who enters a study can introduce {{c1::selection bias}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: A difference in data quality can mimic a biological association.
cards.text: Consistently measuring exposure more thoroughly in one comparison group introduces {{c1::information bias}}.
cards.question: Consistently measuring exposure more thoroughly in one comparison group introduces {{c1::information bias}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The resulting estimate can differ from the true association.
cards.text: Recording a person in the wrong exposure category is exposure {{c1::misclassification}}.
cards.question: Recording a person in the wrong exposure category is exposure {{c1::misclassification}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The observed cohort no longer represents everyone originally enrolled.
cards.text: When participants lost to follow-up differ systematically in outcome risk, estimates may suffer from {{c1::attrition bias}}.
cards.question: When participants lost to follow-up differ systematically in outcome risk, estimates may suffer from {{c1::attrition bias}}.

cards.explanation: Sampling by outcome generally prevents direct calculation of population risks from the sample.
cards.text: The usual association measure in a case–control study is the {{c1::odds ratio}}.
cards.question: The usual association measure in a case–control study is the {{c1::odds ratio}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Divide the odds in cases by the odds in controls. This does not automatically mean double the risk.
cards.text: If exposure odds are 3 among cases and 1.5 among controls, the odds ratio is {{c1::2}}.
cards.question: If exposure odds are 3 among cases and 1.5 among controls, the odds ratio is {{c1::2}}.

cards.explanation: A value of one means equal observed risks over that interval.
cards.text: Dividing cumulative incidence among exposed people by cumulative incidence among unexposed people gives the {{c1::risk ratio}}.
cards.question: Dividing cumulative incidence among exposed people by cumulative incidence among unexposed people gives the {{c1::risk ratio}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The denominator includes all smokers in that group, including those who stayed well.
cards.text: In the smoking cohort, 42 cases among 1,605 smokers gives a cumulative risk of approximately {{c1::2.6%}}.
cards.question: In the smoking cohort, 42 cases among 1,605 smokers gives a cumulative risk of approximately {{c1::2.6%}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Use the unrounded risks. This estimates an association over the observed follow-up.
cards.text: For the slide’s cohort of smokers and non-smokers, (42/1,605) ÷ (46/3,615) gives a risk ratio of about {{c1::2.06}}.
cards.question: For the slide’s cohort of smokers and non-smokers, (42/1,605) ÷ (46/3,615) gives a risk ratio of about {{c1::2.06}}.

cards.explanation: Use those at risk in the exposed group as the denominator.
cards.text: If 15 of 20 exposed nursery children develop chickenpox within 15 days, their attack proportion is {{c1::75%}}.
cards.question: If 15 of 20 exposed nursery children develop chickenpox within 15 days, their attack proportion is {{c1::75%}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: This is the comparison risk for the 15 cases among 20 exposed children.
cards.text: Two of nine unexposed nursery children became ill, giving an unexposed risk of about {{c1::22%}}.
cards.question: Two of nine unexposed nursery children became ill, giving an unexposed risk of about {{c1::22%}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The exposed children had around 3.4 times the observed risk over the same period.
cards.text: Using the nursery data, (15/20) ÷ (2/9) gives a risk ratio of about {{c1::3.38}}.
cards.question: Using the nursery data, (15/20) ÷ (2/9) gives a risk ratio of about {{c1::3.38}}.

cards.explanation: Divide 23 by all 53 exposed children.
cards.text: If 23 exposed children develop gastroenteritis and 30 stay well, the exposed-group risk is about {{c1::43%}}.
cards.question: If 23 exposed children develop gastroenteritis and 30 stay well, the exposed-group risk is about {{c1::43%}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Use the one ill child plus the 42 who remained well as the denominator.
cards.text: If one of 43 unexposed children becomes ill, the attack proportion is about {{c1::2.3%}}.
cards.question: If one of 43 unexposed children becomes ill, the attack proportion is about {{c1::2.3%}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Mean gestational age falls from 33.4 to 31.9 to 30.7 weeks. Group means do not establish individual prognosis.
cards.text: In the retinopathy table, increasing severity is associated with {{c1::lower mean gestational age}}.
cards.question: In the retinopathy table, increasing severity is associated with {{c1::lower mean gestational age}}.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: A placebo or another active treatment may provide the comparator.
cards.text: A study is interventional when the investigator {{c1::assigns the intervention}}.
cards.question: A study is interventional when the investigator {{c1::assigns the intervention}}.

cards.explanation: Chance imbalances remain possible, especially in small trials.
cards.text: In a randomised controlled trial, {{c1::random allocation}} helps balance confounders between treatment groups.
cards.question: In a randomised controlled trial, {{c1::random allocation}} helps balance confounders between treatment groups.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: The relevant comparison depends on how participants were selected.
cards.text: An analytical epidemiological study needs an appropriate {{c1::comparison group}} to evaluate an association.
cards.question: An analytical epidemiological study needs an appropriate {{c1::comparison group}} to evaluate an association.

cards.topic: Choosing a design and interpreting its results
cards.explanation: Baseline exposures are linked to subsequent outcomes.
cards.text: Enrolling women, recording baseline lifestyle and observing later cancer diagnoses is a {{c1::cohort}} design.
cards.question: Enrolling women, recording baseline lifestyle and observing later cancer diagnoses is a {{c1::cohort}} design.

cards.explanation: An epidemic occurs when incidence exceeds what is normally expected in that population.
cards.text: Disease consistently present at its expected level in a region is {{c1::endemic}}.
cards.question: Disease consistently present at its expected level in a region is {{c1::endemic}}.

cards.explanation: The term describes geographic spread.
cards.text: An epidemic extending across multiple countries or continents is termed a {{c1::pandemic}}.
cards.question: An epidemic extending across multiple countries or continents is termed a {{c1::pandemic}}.

cards.explanation: The same count can be ordinary in one setting and exceptional in another.
cards.text: Occurrence above the expected level for a particular population, place and time is an {{c1::epidemic}}.
cards.question: Occurrence above the expected level for a particular population, place and time is an {{c1::epidemic}}.

cards.explanation: First verify the cases and the baseline. Reporting changes can also produce an apparent excess.
cards.text: If a locality normally reports 2–4 cases a week and suddenly reports 13, investigate a possible {{c1::outbreak}}.
cards.question: If a locality normally reports 2–4 cases a week and suddenly reports 13, investigate a possible {{c1::outbreak}}.

cards.explanation: This describes frequency and pattern in a particular setting.
cards.text: Occasional cases with an irregular pattern are described as {{c1::sporadic}}.
cards.question: Occasional cases with an irregular pattern are described as {{c1::sporadic}}.

cards.explanation: The immediate source of a specific exposure can be different.
cards.text: The usual habitat in which an infectious agent persists is its {{c1::reservoir}}.
cards.question: The usual habitat in which an infectious agent persists is its {{c1::reservoir}}.

cards.explanation: Skin and mucosal barriers help protect these sites.
cards.text: The route through which an agent enters a susceptible person is the portal of {{c1::entry}}.
cards.question: The route through which an agent enters a susceptible person is the portal of {{c1::entry}}.

cards.explanation: Disease risk depends on interactions among all three.
cards.text: The epidemiological triad comprises host, agent and {{c1::environment}}.
cards.question: The epidemiological triad comprises host, agent and {{c1::environment}}.

cards.explanation: It helps contain infectious respiratory particles as they leave the patient.
cards.text: Placing a mask on a coughing patient is an example of {{c1::source control}}.
cards.question: Placing a mask on a coughing patient is an example of {{c1::source control}}.

cards.explanation: Intact skin is part of the host’s protection against infection.
cards.text: Preventing skin breakdown preserves a barrier at a potential portal of {{c1::entry}}.
cards.question: Preventing skin breakdown preserves a barrier at a potential portal of {{c1::entry}}.

cards.explanation: Environmental factors describe the surroundings in which host and agent interact.
cards.text: Age and prior immunity are examples of {{c1::host factors}} in the epidemiological triad.
cards.question: Age and prior immunity are examples of {{c1::host factors}} in the epidemiological triad.

cards.explanation: This framework also considers biological, environmental, immunological, nutritional and genetic influences.
cards.text: Within the BEINGS framework, access to healthcare belongs to {{c1::services and social factors}}.
cards.question: Within the BEINGS framework, access to healthcare belongs to {{c1::services and social factors}}.

cards.explanation: Routine clinical counts can underestimate the total burden.
cards.text: The epidemiological iceberg represents the gap between recognised cases and {{c1::subclinical or undetected cases}}.
cards.question: The epidemiological iceberg represents the gap between recognised cases and {{c1::subclinical or undetected cases}}.

cards.explanation: The time of clinical diagnosis can come later still.
cards.text: The interval from infection to the onset of symptoms is the {{c1::incubation period}}.
cards.question: The interval from infection to the onset of symptoms is the {{c1::incubation period}}.

cards.explanation: The absence of recognised symptoms does not establish the absence of infection.
cards.text: A person who harbours an infectious agent without apparent illness can be an asymptomatic {{c1::carrier}}.
cards.question: A person who harbours an infectious agent without apparent illness can be an asymptomatic {{c1::carrier}}.

cards.explanation: Immune individuals reduce opportunities for onward transmission.
cards.text: Susceptible people can gain indirect protection through {{c1::herd immunity}}.
cards.question: Susceptible people can gain indirect protection through {{c1::herd immunity}}.

cards.explanation: Protection against severe symptoms alone does not guarantee the same population effect.
cards.text: Indirect protection from vaccination depends partly on reducing {{c1::onward transmission}}.
cards.question: Indirect protection from vaccination depends partly on reducing {{c1::onward transmission}}.

cards.explanation: A necessary factor may still be insufficient to produce disease by itself.
cards.text: In the sufficient-component cause model, a factor present in every sufficient causal combination is a {{c1::necessary cause}}.
cards.question: In the sufficient-component cause model, a factor present in every sufficient causal combination is a {{c1::necessary cause}}.

cards.explanation: A single component may be present in people who never develop the disease.
cards.text: In Rothman’s causal-pie model, one contributing factor is a {{c1::component cause}}.
cards.question: In Rothman’s causal-pie model, one contributing factor is a {{c1::component cause}}.

cards.explanation: Several different sufficient combinations may lead to the same outcome.
cards.text: A complete set of components that together produces disease constitutes a {{c1::sufficient cause}}.
cards.question: A complete set of components that together produces disease constitutes a {{c1::sufficient cause}}.

cards.explanation: A projection should be interpreted in light of those assumptions and the quality of the data.
cards.text: A mathematical epidemic projection depends on its {{c1::assumptions}} about the population and disease.
cards.question: A mathematical epidemic projection depends on its {{c1::assumptions}} about the population and disease.

cards.explanation: It describes transmission under specified population conditions.
cards.text: The expected number of secondary cases from one typical infectious person in a fully susceptible population is {{c1::R₀}}.
cards.question: The expected number of secondary cases from one typical infectious person in a fully susceptible population is {{c1::R₀}}.

cards.explanation: Individual clusters can still occur even when the average is below one.
cards.text: If the effective reproduction number stays {{c1::below one}}, the expected number of cases falls over successive generations.
cards.question: If the effective reproduction number stays {{c1::below one}}, the expected number of cases falls over successive generations.

cards.explanation: Multiply 3 by 0.5. Above one, incidence can grow under those conditions.

cards.question: If R₀ is 3 and half the population is susceptible, a simple homogeneous-mixing model predicts an effective reproduction number of {{c1::1.5}}.

cards.explanation: Solve 1 = 4 × s. The result assumes homogeneous mixing and effective immunity.
cards.text: With R₀ = 4, an effective reproduction number of one occurs at a susceptible fraction of {{c1::one quarter}} in the simple model.
cards.question: With R₀ = 4, an effective reproduction number of one occurs at a susceptible fraction of {{c1::one quarter}} in the simple model.

cards.explanation: It helps quantify uncertainty around estimates and comparisons.
cards.text: The application of statistical methods to health and biological data is {{c1::biostatistics}}.
cards.question: The application of statistical methods to health and biological data is {{c1::biostatistics}}.

cards.explanation: The denominator is everyone who tests positive, including false positives.
cards.text: The probability of disease given a positive test is its {{c1::positive predictive value}}.
cards.question: The probability of disease given a positive test is its {{c1::positive predictive value}}.

cards.explanation: Among positive results, false positives then make up a larger share.
cards.text: At fixed sensitivity and specificity, a lower disease prevalence generally {{c1::lowers}} positive predictive value.
cards.question: At fixed sensitivity and specificity, a lower disease prevalence generally {{c1::lowers}} positive predictive value.

cards.explanation: Applying consistent criteria makes comparisons across people, places and times interpretable.
cards.text: A standard {{c1::case definition}} specifies who counts as a case in an investigation.
cards.question: A standard {{c1::case definition}} specifies who counts as a case in an investigation.
